1G (Number Theory)

Words: 74 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 74
1G OurBigBook.com
The Chinese remainder theorem says that for pairwise coprime positive moduli m1​,…,ms​, every choice of residues determines exactly one residue class modulo M=∏j​mj​. Equivalently Z/MZ→∏j​Z/mj​Z is an isomorphism under reduction.
The first two modular congruences combine to x=2+15k. Reducing this expression modulo seven gives 2+k≡6, so k=4+7j. Consequently all integer solutions are
x=62+105j,j∈Z.​
(1)
The moduli are pairwise coprime, so the Chinese remainder theorem guarantees that this is the entire solution class.

Define the Lagrange interpolation polynomials
Lj​(x)=∏ℓ=j​xj​−xℓ​x−xℓ​​,Aj​=∫−11​Lj​(x)dx.​
(2)
Distinct interpolation nodes ensure every denominator is nonzero and Lj​(xi​)=δij​. For a polynomial of degree at most n−1, the difference P(x)−∑j​P(xj​)Lj​(x) has degree at most n−1 and vanishes at n distinct points, so it is zero. Integrating this Lagrange interpolation identity proves the required exact quadrature formula. This also covers n=1, when the empty product is one and its weight is two.

ii

Words: 69 Articles: 1
2F OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 69
ii OurBigBook.com
Use Gaussian quadrature: choose the n nodes as the roots of the degree-n Legendre polynomial, which are distinct and inside (−1,1). Retain the integrated Lagrange interpolation weights. With the standard normalization Pn​(1)=1, they can be written
Aj​=(1−xj2​)[Pn′​(xj​)]22​.​
(3)
The orthogonality of the Legendre polynomial against all lower-degree polynomials makes this quadrature exact up to degree 2n−1, twice the arbitrary-node degree apart from the endpoint count. This is the Gauss–Legendre choice of Gaussian quadrature nodes and weights.

3F (Geometry of Group Actions)

Words: 125 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 125
3F OurBigBook.com
For the unit sphere, project from its north pole N=(0,0,1) onto the equatorial plane, identified with the complex plane. The line through N and (X,Y,Z) meets the plane at the stereographic projection
u=1−ZX+iY​,(X,Y,Z)=1+∣u∣2(2Reu,2Imu,∣u∣2−1)​.
(4)
The north pole is omitted from the plane chart; adding its image infinity gives the Riemann sphere.
For a point whose image and antipodal image are finite, stereographic projection of (−X,−Y,−Z) gives v=−(X+iY)/(1+Z). Therefore
uv=−1−Z2X2+Y2​=−1,
(5)
using X2+Y2+Z2=1. Conversely uv=−1 implies v=−1/u. Substituting this into the inverse stereographic projection changes the signs of all three coordinates, proving the converse. Thus finite chart images correspond to antipodes exactly when uv=−1. On the extended chart the exceptional antipodal pair is 0,∞, for which the displayed ordinary complex product is not defined.

4H (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 311 Articles: 6
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

i

Words: 156 Articles: 1
4H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 156
i OurBigBook.com
Each test divides the current candidate set into a tested subset and its complement: failure places the defective item inside the subset, whereas success places it outside. A sequence of tests is therefore a binary decision tree, and minimizing its expected depth is the Huffman coding problem with weights 1,2,…,10.
Combine the smallest two current weights repeatedly. One choice of merges is 1+2=3, 3+3=6, 4+5=9, 6+6=12, 7+8=15, 9+9=18, 10+12=22, 15+18=33, 22+33=55. It gives this explicit prefix code:
itemcode​101110​201111​30110​41110​51111​6010​7100​8101​9110​1000​​
(6)
At any node, test the candidate items whose next code digit is one. Assign failure to digit one and success to digit zero, and repeat until only a single codeword remains. This specifies every test, including the first subset {4,5,7,8,9}. Huffman coding minimizes the weighted codeword lengths, so the optimal expected number is
E[T]=55173​≃3.14545.​
(7)
The sum of the successive merged weights is another check on the numerator 173.

ii

Words: 77 Articles: 1
4H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 77
ii OurBigBook.com
There is a genuinely different optimal procedure. Exchange the codewords assigned to items three and four. Both have code length four, so each item's length, and hence the expected number of tests 173/55, remains unchanged. The first tested subset now contains item three instead of item four, so this changes the tested groups rather than merely reversing the names of the two test outcomes. The new prefix code still identifies every item uniquely and retains the minimum Huffman coding expectation.

iii

Words: 78 Articles: 1
4H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 78
iii OurBigBook.com
The procedure in part (i) sometimes needs five tests, for items one or two. A binary decision tree of height N has at most 2N leaves, so distinguishing ten possibilities requires N≥⌈log2​10⌉=4.
A prefix code attaining this worst-case bound is
itemcode​11100​21101​31110​41111​5000​6001​7010​8011​9100​10101.​​
(8)
Use the same subset-testing rule. The minimum worst-case number is four, so the expected-optimal procedure is not worst-case optimal. This four-test procedure has expectation 175/55, illustrating the small cost of imposing the smaller maximum depth.

Words: 137
5I OurBigBook.com
The logit link gives μi​=eβxi​/(1+eβxi​). Independence in the Bernoulli logistic-regression model therefore gives the log-likelihood
ℓ(β)=i=1∑n​[yi​βxi​−log(1+eβxi​)].​
(9)
Differentiate using dμi​/dβ=xi​μi​(1−μi​):
ℓ′(β)=i∑​xi​(yi​−μi​),ℓ′′(β)=−i∑​xi2​μi​(1−μi​).​
(10)
The maximum-likelihood estimator, if finite, solves the single score equation ∑i​xi​(yi​−μ​i​)=0. If at least one xi​ is nonzero, the log likelihood is strictly concave at finite β, so any root is the unique maximizer.
Use Newton method, equivalently one-parameter iteratively reweighted fitting:
βj+1​=βj​+∑i​xi2​μi​(βj​)[1−μi​(βj​)]∑i​xi​[yi​−μi​(βj​)]​.
(11)
A damped step or a bracketed score solver is useful if a full step overshoots. The finite maximum-likelihood estimate in a one-parameter logistic model requires the score limit at minus infinity to be positive and its limit at plus infinity to be negative. Perfect sign separation of the observations can instead send the estimate to an infinite coefficient; if every xi​=0, the coefficient is unidentifiable. These possibilities should be checked before claiming convergence to a finite estimate.

6A (Mathematical Biology)

Words: 225 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 225
6A OurBigBook.com
In the squared-denominator population map, r is the low-density per-generation multiplication factor, while b controls crowding: 1/b is the characteristic population scale. The nonzero fixed point for r>1 and its multiplier are
N∗​=(r​−1)/b,F′(N∗​)=2/r​−1.​
(12)
Since this multiplier lies strictly between minus one and one, N∗​ is locally asymptotically stable. This holds for every finite r>1, even when the map is locally decreasing at its fixed point.
For the post-initial invariant interval for a squared-denominator population map, put M=r/(4b) and L=4r2/[b(r+4)2]. The derivative F′(N)=r(1−bN)/(1+bN)3 shows that the global maximum is M at N=1/b. The first two iterates of the supplied initial condition are consequently
N2​=M,N3​=F(M)=L.
(13)
For r>4, 1/b<L≤M. Hence the map decreases throughout [L,M], with minimum F(M)=L there, and its global maximum bound ensures F(L)≤M. Thus F([L,M])⊆[L,M], and induction proves
L≤Nt​≤Mfor every t≥2.​
(14)
Both endpoints are attained at t=2,3. The lower bound printed without a time qualification is false at t=1, because the given value N1​=1/b is strictly below L when r>4. The invariant bounds apply after that initial step, not to it.
The cobweb plot below uses n=bN and r=9. The first vertical move reaches the maximum, the next reaches its image, and subsequent vertical/horizontal steps remain in the invariant interval and approach the stable fixed point.

7E (Dynamical Systems)

Words: 230 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 230
7E OurBigBook.com
A Lyapunov function near an equilibrium is a continuously differentiable function with V(0)=0, V(x)>0 for nonzero nearby x, and V˙=∇V⋅f≤0 along trajectories there. Strict negativity away from the equilibrium gives local asymptotic stability. Lyapunov stability itself means that every prescribed small neighborhood contains a smaller neighborhood whose forward trajectories never leave the prescribed one.
For the proposed quadratic form, direct differentiation gives
V˙=−2[(x−y)2+(β−1)y2]+4x2y−2x3+(2β−8)xy2.
(15)
When β>1, the quadratic part is negative definite, so it dominates the cubic remainder in a sufficiently small ball; V is then a strict Lyapunov function. If 0<β<1, take x=y to make the leading derivative positive. At β=1, that same line gives V˙=−4x3, positive on its negative half. Values β≤0 fail positive definiteness of V. Therefore
β>1.​
(16)
For β=2 the full derivative factors, with no small-amplitude truncation:
V˙=−2(1+x)[(x−y)2+y2],V=x2+2y2.
(17)
Every closed sublevel set V≤c<1 lies in x>−1, is forward invariant, and has strictly decreasing V away from the origin. Compactness and the Lyapunov stability argument therefore show that the ellipse x2+2y2<1 belongs to the origin's basin of attraction. Boundary points with V=1 other than (−1,0) also have negative derivative and enter the ellipse. The exception (−1,0) is another fixed point, so the largest such sublevel ellipse cannot be included wholesale in the basin. This is a basin estimate from a Lyapunov sublevel set, not a claim that no additional points outside the ellipse converge to the origin.

8B (Further Complex Methods)

Words: 152 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 152
8B OurBigBook.com
Normalize the second-order equation as y′′+P(z)y′+Q(z)y=0, with P,Q holomorphic at all finite nonzero points. The regular singular point criterion for a second-order equation at zero says that zP(z) and z2Q(z) extend holomorphically across zero.
To impose the condition at infinity, set w=1/z and Y(w)=y(1/w). Since y′=−w2Y′ and y′′=w4Y′′+2w3Y′, the transformed equation is
Y′′+(w2​−w2P(1/w)​)Y′+w4Q(1/w)​Y=0.
(18)
Regular singularity at w=0 makes 2−P(1/w)/w and Q(1/w)/w2 bounded and holomorphic there. Equivalently zP(z) and z2Q(z) are bounded at infinity. They are entire functions by the zero-endpoint condition, so Liouville's theorem makes both constants. The Euler-Cauchy classification from two regular singular points is therefore
z2y′′+Azy′+By=0,A,B∈C.​
(19)
Conversely these equations have ordinary coefficients everywhere on C∗ and meet both regular-singularity bounds. If “regular singular” is required to exclude an ordinary point, omit (A,B)=(0,0), which makes zero ordinary, and (2,0), which makes infinity ordinary. Under the common “at worst regular singular” convention these two cases are included. Multiplication by a nonvanishing coefficient does not change the normalized equation or this classification.

9E (Classical Dynamics)

Words: 169 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 169
9E OurBigBook.com
Assume the velocity-to-momentum Legendre map is locally invertible. Differentiate the Hamiltonian while regarding q,p,t as independent:
dH=∑i​q˙​i​dpi​+∑i​pi​dq˙​i​−dL=∑i​q˙​i​dpi​−∑i​∂qi​∂L​dqi​−∂t∂L​dt.
(20)
The velocity variations cancel because pi​=∂L/∂q˙​i​. Combining the remaining coefficients with the Euler-Lagrange equations gives Hamilton's equations
q˙​i​=∂pi​∂H​,p˙​i​=−∂qi​∂H​.​
(21)
An ignorable coordinate does not occur explicitly in the Lagrangian, so its conjugate momentum is conserved. For the spherical motion, ϕ is ignorable and the Hamiltonian has no explicit time dependence. The two constants are pϕ​ and H.
The polar Hamilton equations are
θ˙=ma2pθ​​,p˙​θ​=ma2sin3θpϕ2​cosθ​−V′(θ).
(22)
A constant polar angle therefore requires pθ​=0 and vanishing of the second right-hand side. For 0<θ<π with cosθ=0, this is
pϕ2​=cosθma2sin3θ​V′(θ).​
(23)
The expression must be nonnegative to represent a real momentum. Once it holds, ϕ advances uniformly at pϕ​/(ma2sin2θ), so it is also sufficient with those initial data. At the equator the undivided equation instead requires V′(π/2)=0, with any pϕ​; dividing by cosine would wrongly discard this special case. The polar coordinate chart itself excludes the poles.

10D (Cosmology)

Words: 203 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 203
10D OurBigBook.com
Assume dilute nondegenerate nonrelativistic particles, a common temperature, chemical equilibrium, charge neutrality np​=ne​, and photons with zero chemical potential. The reaction balance gives μp​+μe​=μH​. Dividing the two charged-species equilibrium densities by the neutral density cancels their chemical-potential factors and leaves
nH​np​ne​​=gH​gp​ge​​(h22πkT​mH​mp​me​​)3/2exp[−kT(mp​+me​−mH​)c2​].
(24)
For ground-state hydrogen, gp​=ge​=2 and gH​=4, and mH​≃mp​ in the thermal prefactor. The rest-mass difference is I/c2. These approximations give the Saha ionization equation
nH​ne2​​=(h22πme​kT​)3/2e−I/(kT).​
(25)
Excited levels or different degeneracy conventions would change the prefactor; the stated assumptions give the printed normalization.
Write the right side as S(T). Since ne​=Xe​nB​ and nH​=(1−Xe​)nB​, the hydrogen ionization fraction obeys Xe2​/(1−Xe​)=S(T)/nB​. With nB​=ηnγ​, the given blackbody photon density then yields
Xe2​1−Xe​​=π​42​ζ(3)​η(me​c2kT​)3/2eI/(kT).​
(26)
There are vastly more photons than baryons. Even when the typical photon energy is below the ionization energy, the high-energy tail can contain enough ionizing photons to keep nearly every baryon ionized. Neutral hydrogen forms only when that tail becomes sufficiently depleted relative to the very small baryon-to-photon ratio. This entropy/number-density effect explains why cosmological recombination occurs at a temperature far below I, rather than simply when kT first falls below the binding energy. The Saha ionization equation describes the equilibrium estimate; late kinetic freeze-out is a separate limitation of that approximation.

11F (Geometry of Group Actions)

Words: 303 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 303
11F OurBigBook.com
A frieze group is a discrete subgroup of Euclidean isometries whose translation subgroup is generated by one nonzero vector and has finite index. A plane crystallographic group is a discrete subgroup of Euclidean isometries with a rank-two translation lattice of finite index; equivalently its action has a compact fundamental region.
Here are three frieze groups, with explicit generators. The translation T(x,y)=(x+1,y) alone gives Z. Adding the vertical reflection in mathematics S(x,y)=(−x,y) gives Z⋊C2​, the infinite dihedral group, since STS=T−1. Instead adding the horizontal reflection in mathematics H(x,y)=(x,−y) gives Z×C2​, since HT=TH. Their translation parts are exactly ⟨T⟩ and their point parts have respectively one, two and two elements.
For plane crystallographic groups, let T1​(x,y)=(x+1,y) and T2​(x,y)=(x,y+1). These generate Z2. Adding the half-turn R2​(x,y)=(−x,−y) gives Z2⋊C2​, with inversion on both translation generators. Adding the quarter-turn R4​(x,y)=(−y,x) gives Z2⋊C4​, with R4​T1​R4−1​=T2​ and R4​T2​R4−1​=T1−1​. These are the translation, half-turn and square-rotation wallpaper groups. Integer translation vectors and a finite point part make each group a discrete subgroup; the unit square meets every orbit, establishing a cocompact group action.
For the final claim, suppose a Euclidean isometry R has order five. An orientation-reversing planar isometry has finite order only when it is a reflection in mathematics, so R is a rotation through θ=2πj/5, j=1,2,3,4, about some centre. Write A for its linear rotation part. If tv​∈G is a nonzero translation, conjugation gives Rtv​R−1=tAv​. Thus G contains translations by v and by (A+A−1)v=cv, where c=2cosθ.
For a primitive fifth root ζ, dividing 1+ζ+ζ2+ζ3+ζ4=0 by ζ2 gives c2+c−1=0. Hence c is irrational. The pigeonhole principle, applied to N+1 fractional parts of 0,c,…,Nc in N equal intervals, gives integers m,n with 0<∣nc−m∣≤1/N. Consequently G contains nonidentity translations by (nc−m)v tending to the identity. This contradicts the discrete subgroup hypothesis. There is no element of order five. This argument needs only the given nonzero translation, not a rank-two lattice.

For probability distributions p,q with positive entries, Gibbs inequality is
D(p∥q)=∑j​pj​logqj​pj​​≥0,
(27)
with equality exactly when p=q. Indeed, logx≤x−1, with equality only at x=1, gives
−D(p∥q)=∑j​pj​log(qj​/pj​)≤∑j​(qj​−pj​)=0.
(28)
This also proves the equality condition. With zero entries the same Kullback-Leibler divergence statement holds using 0log(0/q)=0 and plog(p/0)=+∞ for p>0, or by restricting to the support and taking limits.

ii

Words: 85 Articles: 1
12H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 85
ii OurBigBook.com
Let J1​,J2​,… be independent rolls with the specified probability distribution, and let Fm​ be the fortune after m games. Its multiplicative evolution gives
m1​logfFm​​=m1​∑ν=1m​loguJν​​aJν​​​⟶g(a)=∑j​pj​loguj​aj​​almost surely,
(29)
by the strong law of large numbers. The summands have finitely many finite values, so its hypotheses hold. For any ε>0, the probability that fem(g−ε)≤Fm​≤fem(g+ε) tends to one. Thus maximizing g(a) maximizes the typical exponential growth rate, the objective of log-optimal multiplicative betting. Maximizing expected fortune would be a different objective and would not control the typical repeated-game outcome.

iii

Words: 119 Articles: 1
12H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 119
iii OurBigBook.com
By Gibbs inequality,
g(a)=∑j​pj​loguj​pj​​−D(p∥a)≤∑j​pj​loguj​pj​​,
(30)
with equality exactly when aj​=pj​​. Put qj​=uj​/U, a probability distribution. The optimal log-optimal multiplicative betting rate is
g∗​=D(p∥q)−logU.​
(31)
For U<1 this is strictly positive by Gibbs inequality; taking 0<ε<g∗​ in the preceding strong law of large numbers bound proves growth with probability tending to one.
For U>1 the casino can set uj​=Upj​. Every optimal return multiplier is then exactly 1/U, so the fortune decreases deterministically as fU−m. More generally g∗​=−logU<0 for that choice. An arbitrary choice with U>1 need not cause decline. For example, take p1​=p2​=1/2, u1​=0.01, u2​=1.99. Then U=2 but g∗​=(1/2)log[0.25/(0.01⋅1.99)]>0. For any fixed positive p, making one uj​ sufficiently small while preserving U also makes the optimal rate positive.

13I (Statistical Modelling)

Words: 446 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 446
13I OurBigBook.com
The first fit is grouped-binomial logistic regression: independently, Yi​∼Bin(Ni​,πi​), with the observed group sizes Ni​ and
log1−πi​πi​​=β0​+β1​I50–69,i​+β2​I70+,i​+β3​Imalignant,i​.
(32)
The reference group is under 50 with a nonmalignant initial tumour. The weights specify binomial numbers of trials, not six equally weighted individual observations. There is no age-by-malignancy interaction. Each age coefficient compares that age group with the reference age at fixed malignancy; expβ3​ is the common malignancy odds ratio.
The maximum-likelihood estimates are obtained by maximizing the binomial likelihood. The reported standard errors come from the inverse fitted Fisher information. Each displayed Wald test tests a coefficient equal to zero, using z=β​/se(β​) and the approximate standard normal distribution; its two-sided probability is 2Φ(−∣z∣). At the 5% level the middle age coefficient and the malignancy coefficient are significant, with negative signs; the oldest age coefficient is not, although its 9.17% probability is weaker evidence in the same direction. The oldest group has only 19 observations and its larger standard error does not establish absence of an age effect. The intercept tests reference log-odds zero, equivalently reference survival probability 1/2, rather than an age contrast. The reference fitted probability is about 0.888; the fitted malignancy odds ratio is about 0.481.
The binomial deviance is twice the saturated-minus-fitted log-likelihood. The null fit has one parameter, hence 6−1=5 residual degrees of freedom; the first fit has four parameters, hence 6−4=2. The improvement 12.65585−0.49409=12.16176 is an approximate likelihood-ratio test on three degrees of freedom, with probability about 0.0069. The residual deviance 0.49409, compared with χ22​, gives about 0.781, so there is no evidence of lack of fit. These are asymptotic comparisons, especially approximate for the small oldest strata. The Akaike information criterion is −2ℓ+2p, here with p=4.
Pooling the two older age groups gives a grouped-binomial logistic regression with a common coefficient for age at least 50 and three parameters in total. The similar older-age estimates and the sparse oldest group motivate examining this restriction, but the significance of either coefficient separately is not a test of their equality. The actual analysis of deviance for pooling compares the nested fits: the deviance increases by only 0.784−0.49409≃0.28991 for one lost parameter, giving a χ12​ probability about 0.590. The pooled model also has smaller Akaike information criterion, 28.723 rather than 30.433. Prefer the pooled model for its simpler adequate fit. Call a set function f with ordinal domain γ good if f(ξ)=G(ξ,ran(f∣ξ​)) for every ξ<γ. Any two good functions agree on their common domain: otherwise their first disagreement has identical earlier ranges and hence identical values under G. This is transfinite induction, not an assumption of the desired recursion.
Good functions exist with every ordinal domain. At a successor stage extend the unique previous function by its prescribed value under G. At a limit stage, Axiom schema of replacement collects the unique good functions on all smaller domains into a set, and their compatible union is a good function on the limit domain. Each earlier range is a set, so G is applied only to sets. Transfinite induction now establishes existence at all stages. Define F(α) to be the value at α of the unique good function on α+1. An initial ordinal is an ordinal not bijective with any smaller ordinal. It is the canonical ordinal representative of a well-orderable cardinal, so cardinal arithmetic can be defined by taking the initial ordinal equinumerous with a disjoint union, Cartesian product or function set. In the usual setting with the axiom of choice, every cardinal has such a representative. Hartogs theorem says that for every set A there is an ordinal h(A) which does not inject into A, and there is a least such ordinal. For an initial ordinal κ it is the next larger initial ordinal: every smaller ordinal injects into κ, and if h(κ) were equinumerous with a smaller ordinal it too would inject into κ.
Use the recursion just proved to set ω0​=ω, ωβ+1​=h(ωβ​) and ωλ​=supβ<λ​ωβ​ for nonzero limit λ. These instructions use the earlier value set alone: at a successor it has a maximum, and at a limit its supremum is taken. They are therefore implemented by an appropriate definable G. The limit supremum is initial: if it were bijective with γ below it, choose an earlier ωβ​>γ; then ωβ​ would inject into γ, contradicting initiality. The sequence is strictly increasing and continuous. There are no omitted infinite initial ordinals, since each successor chooses the least next one and each limit is the supremum; more formally, a least omitted initial ordinal cannot lie between successive terms, and the least term above it cannot be a limit term. Terms eventually exceed any prescribed ordinal, since a strictly increasing ordinal sequence satisfies ωβ​≥β.

Hall's marriage theorem states that a finite bipartite graph with parts A,B has a matching in a graph saturating A exactly when ∣N(S)∣≥∣S∣ for every S⊆A. Necessity follows because the matched neighbours of S are distinct.
For sufficiency use induction on ∣A∣. The empty case is immediate. If a nonempty proper subset S has ∣N(S)∣=∣S∣, the induced graph on S,N(S) satisfies Hall's condition and has a saturating matching in a graph by induction. The remaining graph on A∖S,B∖N(S) also satisfies it: for T⊆A∖S,
∣N(T)∖N(S)∣=∣N(T∪S)∣−∣N(S)∣≥∣T∣.
(45)
Apply induction again and unite the two matchings in a graph. If there is no such tight proper subset, every nonempty proper S has ∣N(S)∣≥∣S∣+1. Choose a vertex a and a neighbour b, which exists by Hall's condition. Delete both. Every remaining subset loses at most one neighbour and still satisfies Hall's condition. Induction supplies a matching in a graph of the remainder; add ab. For ∣A∣=1 this last step directly proves the assertion.

Every vertex outside S therefore sends all its k edges into S, giving k(n−2m) crossing edges. Every vertex in S already uses at least one incident edge inside S, its matched edge, so it sends at most k−1 outside. Hence
k(n−2m)≤2m(k−1),m≥4k−2kn​.​

A K-isomorphism L→L′ is a field isomorphism fixing every element of K. The field automorphism group AutK​(L) consists of such isomorphisms L→L, with composition.
If an isomorphism sends α to β, it takes every polynomial relation over K for α to the same relation for β; the monic minimal polynomials coincide. Conversely, if their common minimal polynomial is m, evaluation induces field isomorphisms K[X]/(m)≅K(α) and K[X]/(m)≅K(β). Their composite sends α to β and fixes K.
An automorphism of K(α) sends α to a root of m inside K(α) and is determined by this image. More precisely the field automorphism group permutes the set of roots of m lying in this field, a set of size s≤d. This action is faithful because fixing α fixes the generated field. Thus AutK​(K(α)) embeds in Ss​, and then in Sd​ by fixing d−s extra labels. In particular it is finite. This argument also covers inseparable minimal polynomials.
For an example not isomorphic even as abstract fields, take K=Fp​(t), let α generate Fpp​ over Fp​, and put β=t1/p. The constant-field minimal polynomial of α remains irreducible over the rational function field: if it factored over Fp​(t), each monic factor's coefficients would be algebraic over Fp​, being symmetric functions of constant algebraic roots. A rational function algebraic over Fp​ is constant, so those coefficients would lie in Fp​, contradicting the original irreducibility. The polynomial Xp−t is irreducible by Eisenstein criterion at t in Fp​[t]. Both degrees are p, but
K(α)=Fpp​(t),K(β)=Fp​(β).
(47)
The first field has pp roots of Xpp−X; the second has only p. Indeed a rational function algebraic over a finite constant field must be constant: a nonconstant rational function makes the transcendental variable algebraic over its own rational-function field, and therefore cannot itself be algebraic over the constants. The root counts are isomorphism invariants. These extensions are not isomorphic.
If K=Fq​ is finite, every degree-d extension is a field with qd elements. Such fields are splitting fields of Xqd−X over K, so uniqueness of the splitting field gives a K-isomorphism. There is no finite-base-field example of this kind.

The Baire category theorem states that a complete metric space is a Baire space: the intersection of countably many open dense sets is dense. Equivalently, a nonempty open subset cannot be a countable union of nowhere dense sets.
Let Un​ be open dense and O any nonempty open set. Choose a closed ball B1​ of positive radius at most 1/2 inside O∩U1​. Inductively choose Bn+1​ inside the interior of Bn​ intersected with Un+1​, with positive radius at most 2−(n+1). Density makes this intersection nonempty, and openness supplies a sufficiently small closed ball. The centres form a Cauchy sequence because all later centres lie in Bn​, whose diameter tends to zero. Completeness gives a limit x. Since each ball is closed and contains all later centres, x∈Bn​ for every n. Thus x∈O∩⋂n​Un​, proving density. Applying this to complements of the closures of nowhere dense sets gives the equivalent formulation.

It can be represented there by rational homogeneous coordinate functions not all zero. A point is regular for the map if it extends as a morphism on an open neighbourhood of that point.
For the given projective Cremona transformation, the three products vanish simultaneously exactly at the three coordinate vertices. Away from them they define a regular map. At (1:0:0) consider [1:t:st] as t→0, with s=0. Its image tends to [0:s:1], which depends on s. No regular extension could have these different limiting values. Algebraically these curves lie in its domain for t=0 and a regular extension must give the same specialization at their common vertex, so the obstruction also works over any infinite characteristic-zero field. A smooth plane curve is geometrically irreducible: if it had two positive-degree components, Bézout theorem over the algebraic closure would give an intersection point, and the product equation has zero gradient there; a repeated factor also makes the gradient vanish along its component. Therefore this quartic is irreducible. Its torus part is dense and is identified by the projective Cremona transformation with the torus part of V. No coordinate line is a component of V, since restricting F to each coordinate line leaves a nonzero monomial. Consequently every component meets the torus, and its torus part is already irreducible. V is irreducible and birational to the nonsingular quartic AC3+A3B+B3C=0.

Since the degree of a map between oriented manifolds is invariant under smooth homotopy, f is not smoothly homotopic to the identity. For n=0, the symmetry makes f constant on the two-point discrete sphere; a continuous homotopy into this discrete space cannot change either point's image, so the conclusion still holds.

A simple function is a measurable function with finitely many values, written s=∑j=1m​aj​1Aj​​ using disjoint measurable sets. For nonnegative s its Lebesgue integral is μ(s)=∑j​aj​μ(Aj​), with 0⋅∞=0. An integrable signed simple function has ∑j​∣aj​∣μ(Aj​)<∞ and the same signed sum defines its integral.
For a nonnegative measurable f define μ(f)=sup{μ(s):s simple, 0≤s≤f}. A real measurable f is Lebesgue integrable when μ(∣f∣)<∞; then μ(f)=μ(f+)−μ(f−), both terms finite. The monotone convergence theorem states that if 0≤fn​↑f pointwise, or almost everywhere, then μ(fn​)↑μ(f), allowing infinity.
For nonnegative f,g, choose nonnegative simple approximations sn​↑f, tn​↑g. Their sums increase to f+g; simple-function additivity and monotone convergence give μ(f+g)=μ(f)+μ(g). The same approximation proves μ(cf)=cμ(f) for c≥0.
For integrable signed f,g, ∣f+g∣≤∣f∣+∣g∣ makes their sum integrable. Write u=f++g+, v=f−+g−. The identity u+(f+g)−=v+(f+g)+ and nonnegative additivity, with finite integrals, give μ(f+g)=μ(f)+μ(g). Also (cf)±=cf± when c≥0, while negative c interchanges the two parts, so μ(cf)=cμ(f) for every real c. Integrals do not change upon alteration on a null set, hence this descends to Lebesgue space. The indicated map is linear.

Fix M. Each time the chain is in {1,…,M} immediately before a jump, its conditional chance to jump to zero is at least the δ from part (b). Count all these opportunities, including returns to the same state after an excursion; the Tm​ in part (b) need not count those returns. By the Strong Markov property at successive such visits, the probability of surviving r opportunities without absorption is at most (1−δ)r. Hence infinitely many such opportunities without hitting zero have probability zero.
A positive state cannot be occupied forever: its finite positive holding rate gives an almost surely finite holding time. For a nonexplosive continuous-time Markov chain, visits at arbitrarily late times to the finite set therefore require infinitely many of the counted opportunities. On the event of no absorption, the chain consequently eventually stays above M, almost surely. Intersect this probability-one assertion over integers M. The result is Xt​→∞. If zero is ever reached it remains occupied forever, and for initial state zero this is immediate. Thus Pi​(E∪F)=1​ for every initial state.
This uses the usual assumption implicit in an I-valued chain defined for all t≥0: no explosion with loss to a cemetery state. The rate conditions alone do not ensure it. Choose u solving □u=R/2, using the granted solvability, and let Ω=eu>0. The stated conformal transformation formula gives R=0. The one-component result makes the full curvature zero. A flat Lorentzian metric is locally isometric to Minkowski spacetime: parallel transport on a simply connected small neighbourhood supplies a parallel orthonormal frame, whose closed dual coframe integrates to flat coordinates. This is a local conclusion; vanishing curvature does not supply global Minkowski coordinates on an arbitrary topology.
In local two-dimensional Minkowski coordinates U=T−X, V=T+X, a regular smooth null curve obeys U′V′=0. Its nonzero continuous tangent stays on one of the two null directions locally, hence the curve lies on U=constant or V=constant, a straight null line. It is a reparameterized null geodesic. Conformal invariance proves that every regular null curve in the original two-dimensional metric is a null geodesic, without requiring global flat coordinates.
For the displayed metric put u=log∣t∣. When t>0, ds2=t(−du2+dθ2); when t<0, ds2=∣t∣(du2−dθ2). In both cases the two null families are
θ=±log∣t∣+θ0​.​
(94)
If θ is angular, the endpoints 0,2π are identified and these wind repeatedly around the cylinder as t→0 and as ∣t∣→∞. To find the original affine behaviour, the Killing momentum ℓ=tθ˙ is constant and the null condition gives t˙2=ℓ2. A nontrivial null curve has ℓ=0, so t is affine-linear: it reaches the excluded boundary t=0 in finite affine time despite infinitely many windings, and reaches ∣t∣=∞ only in infinite affine time.
The metric is already locally flat. For t>0, set T=2t​cosh(θ/2), X=2t​sinh(θ/2); for t<0 interchange the hyperbolic sine and cosine with 2∣t∣​. Both give ds2=−dT2+dX2. The angular identification acts as a Lorentz boost, so these are not global single-valued Minkowski coordinates. Constant-t circles are spacelike for t>0 and timelike for t<0; the negative branch therefore has closed timelike curves, though its null curves continue to change t. If the angular endpoints are not identified, the formulas describe the corresponding unwrapped strips instead. This exhibits concretely the local/global qualification in the earlier request.

Lubrication theory exploits a film thickness b much smaller than its horizontal variation scale ℓ. Incompressibility then gives vertical velocity of order (b/ℓ)U, vertical viscous derivatives dominate horizontal ones, and inertia is negligible when ρUb2/(μℓ)≪1. The leading equations reduce to μuyy​=px​ and vertical hydrostatic balance py​=−ρg. Boundary conditions determine the local horizontal velocity profile; integrating it across the film and enforcing mass conservation produces an equation for flux or surface shape. This reduction turns the thin-film problem into a one-dimensional pressure problem while retaining the dominant viscous stresses.

u(x,y)=U+2μpx​​(y2−d2),Q=Ud−3μd3px​​.​

0=∫−∞∞​px​dx=3μ[U∫d−2dx−Q∫d−3dx].

For spherical symmetry, rp​ satisfies the one-dimensional wave equation, so an outgoing solution has the form A(t−r/c)/r. To relate A to the source, use a velocity potential Φ with ur​=∂r​Φ and p​=−ρ∂t​Φ. The outgoing monopole potential
Φ=−4πρrq(t−r/c)​
(101)
has 4πr2ρur​→q(t) as r→0, fixing its mass-flux normalization. It follows that
p​(r,t)=4πrq′(t−r/c)​.​
(102)
For an element with displacement f0​eiωt, its volume outflow is iωf0​h2eiωt and mass outflow is ρ times this. Thus q′=−ρω2f0​h2eiωt. A rigid wall imposes zero normal velocity away from the source. The method of images uses a source of the same sign on the other side; a source on the plane and its image coincide, doubling the full-space monopole field. Equivalently its mass flux spreads over a hemisphere rather than a sphere. Hence
p​=−4πR2ρω2f0​h2​eiω(t−R/c).​
(103)
The small patch relative to wavelength justifies the point source, and the small displacement justifies linear acoustics.
Superposition over the aperture gives the Rayleigh integral for baffled acoustic radiation
p​(t,x,y,z)=−2πρω2​∬Rf(y′,z′)​eiω(t−R/c)dy′dz′,R=x2+(y−y′)2+(z−z′)2​.
(104)
For r≫L, R=r−(yy′+zz′)/r+O(L2/r) and R−1=r−1[1+O(L/r)]. The additional condition r≫ωL2/c makes the omitted phase small, so with the printed Fourier transform convention
p​≃−2πrρω2​eiω(t−r/c)f​(m,n),m=−rcωy​,n=−rcωz​.​
(105)
The minus signs in m,n arise because the outgoing phase contributes +iω(yy′+zz′)/(rc).
For the rectangle the two integrals factor, giving
f​(m,n)=mn4sin(am)sin(bn)​=4absinc(am)sinc(bn),​
(106)
where sincu=sinu/u and its zero-argument limit is one. If k=ω/c, kb≪1 implies ∣bn∣≤kb≪1, so the z-direction factor is nearly one throughout the radiation hemisphere. With ka of order one the y-direction factor varies appreciably: the long dimension gives stronger directivity in that angular direction, while the short dimension radiates broadly. The forward amplitude is proportional to the area 4ab. Nulls have kay/r equal to nonzero integer multiples of π when those values are physically accessible; order-one ka does not automatically imply that the first null lies in the hemisphere.

For a fixed n, convergence for every initial error is equivalent to ∣1−ωtk​∣<1 for all k, where tk​=1−cos(kπ/(n+1))>0. Thus
0<ω<1+cos(π/(n+1))2​=cos2(π/[2(n+1)])1​.
(110)
A single parameter works for every finite n precisely when 0<ω≤1​: the largest tk​ tends to two as n→∞, so every ω>1 eventually fails, whereas ω=1 has all eigenvalues strictly between −1 and one for each finite grid.
For such ω the lowest-frequency eigenvalue satisfies, using 1−cosx≤x2/2,
λ1​(ω)=1−ω(1−cos(π/(n+1)))≥1−2(n+1)2π2​.
(111)
An initial error proportional to v1​ retains exactly the factor λ1ν​. Hence the worst-case spectral radius cannot improve on a factor of the form (1−c/n2)ν, with c independent of grid size, and reducing a slow-mode error by a fixed fraction takes order n2 iterations. This is a worst-case rate assertion, not a lower bound for every individual initial error: a vector containing only faster modes, or the zero vector, need not exhibit the slow mode.

Let k0​=⌈(n+1)/2⌉, θ=π/(n+1), and define the high-frequency endpoint parameters
a=1−cos(k0​θ),b=1+cosθ.
(112)
They obey 1≤a≤b<2 (with equality of endpoints for a single high mode). Since ∣1−ωt∣ is convex in t and the endpoint modes are included, the exact high-frequency attenuation is
μω​=max{∣1−ωa∣,∣1−ωb∣}.
(113)
The minimax choice balances the endpoint values with opposite signs. If they were not balanced, moving ω toward their balancing point would lower the larger endpoint value. Thus
ω∗(n)​=a+b2​,μ∗(n)​=a+bb−a​.​
(114)
For odd n, a=1, giving ω∗​=2/(2+cosθ) and μ∗​=cosθ/(2+cosθ). For even n, a=1+sin(θ/2), giving
ω∗(n)​=2+cosθ+sin(θ/2)2​,μ∗(n)​=2+cosθ+sin(θ/2)cosθ−sin(θ/2)​.
(115)
These give the exact finite-grid high-frequency Jacobi smoothing optimum, including complete annihilation when there is only one high-frequency mode. Their grid-independent limits are ω∗​=2/3, μ∗​=1/3​. Choosing 2/3 damps every high mode by at most 1/3 on every grid, while its low-mode factor remains 1−O(n−2). Thus high frequencies decay geometrically much faster. The familiar 2/3,1/3 pair is the optimal uniform-in-grid smoother; it need not be the exact optimum on a particular finite sine-mode grid.
